interactive.title: The arrow that slides
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on one grid with one arrow, a, drawn from its tail to its tip. A readout beside it gives its two moves, how many squares across and how many up from tail to tip, with left and down as minus, and its size, the arrow's length. The size comes from Pythagoras, because the across and up moves are at right angles: √(3² + 4²) = 5 for the opening arrow. Dragging the tip sets the moves, so the size and direction change. Dragging the arrow's middle slides the whole arrow, while a faint copy stays at the origin. The readout does not change, because the moves are the same, and the copy matches. A scale slider from −3 to 3 multiplies both moves by its number. The arrow stretches, shrinks to a dot at 0 and comes out the other way below 0. Its size is the number, without its sign, times the starting size. A Unit button divides both moves by the size, leaving an arrow of length 1 along the same line. One screen shows a pump with its mass as a plain number and its weight as an arrow pointing down. One shows four arrows in different places. One marks two points, A and B, with the arrows AB and BA between them. One shows a boat going round a circle at a steady speed, its velocity arrow turning as it goes. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is drawn on the grid so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: The grid's squares have no unit, so the same arrow can stand for metres, newtons or knots. Sliding an arrow keeps the vector the same, but a real force also acts at a point on a body, and where it acts matters when it turns the body. That comes with turning, later on. The puzzles' numbers are example values chosen to give whole numbers or short decimals. Directions here lie flat on the page, and a vector can just as well point up out of it.

explain.text:
A [[vector]] is a size with a direction.[^1] A force, a velocity and an acceleration are all vectors. You draw one as an arrow. Its length is the size and the way it points is the direction. A quantity with a size and no direction, such as mass, energy or temperature, is a [[scalar]]. A pump's 500 kg mass is a scalar. Its weight is a vector, because weight is a force that pulls it down.

On a grid, the arrow called a runs 3 squares across and 4 up from its tail to its tip. The two moves are at right angles, so the arrow is the long side of a right-angled triangle. Pythagoras gives its size: √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5, written |a| = 5. Size and direction are all the arrow holds, so where it is drawn is not part of it. Two arrows with the same size and direction are the same vector, wherever they sit.[^2] Slide a anywhere on the grid and it still runs 3 across and 4 up, so it is still a. The arrow from point A to point B is the vector AB. Going from B back to A covers the same ground the other way. Moving backwards along a vector makes it negative,[^3] so BA = −AB. In print a vector's letter is bold, and by hand it is underlined.

A number in front scales a vector. 2a is a done twice, 3 across and 4 up and then the same again. So it runs 6 across and 8 up, the same way and twice as long, size 10. Each move is multiplied, so the triangle grows in proportion and the direction holds. A negative number also turns the arrow round, because making a vector negative reverses its direction.[^4] So −2a runs 6 left and 8 down. Its size is still 10, because a length cannot be below zero. The arrows a, 2a and −2a lie along one line, so they are parallel. Dividing a by its own size, 5, shrinks it to length 1 the same way. That is its [[unit vector]], 0.6 across and 0.8 up, and it holds the direction alone. Because direction is part of every vector, two of them cannot be added just by adding their sizes.[^5] Each line current has an angle too, which is why 10 A, 10 A and 4 A on a three-phase board need not put 24 A on the neutral.

**A vector is only its size and its direction, so its arrow can be drawn anywhere,[^2] and a number in front stretches or shrinks it and, if negative, turns it round.**

analogy.text: Running conduit up a stair wall, you might set each saddle 300 mm across and 400 mm up from the last. That step is the same move wherever you start it, so it is one vector, and its length is 500 mm. Three saddles on is three times the step, 900 mm across and 1,200 mm up. Coming back down is the step reversed.
analogy.breaks: A step on a wall is a distance, but a vector can just as well be a force or a velocity, where the arrow's length stands for newtons or knots. And a real force pushes at one place on a body, which matters when it turns it, though the vector itself is still only its size and direction.

practice.text:
- Read the moves from tail to tip: across first, then up. Left and down are minus.
- Find the size by Pythagoras on the two moves.
- To compare two vectors, compare their moves, never where they sit.
- To reverse a vector, change the sign of both moves. To scale it, multiply both moves by the number.
- For the unit vector, divide both moves by the size, then check its size comes out as 1.

**Rule of thumb:** Same moves, same vector. A minus in front turns it round.

**Worked example:** A boat's velocity v is 3 m/s east and 4 m/s north. Its speed is the size, √(3² + 4²) = 5 m/s. At half speed on the same heading, ½v is 1.5 m/s east and 2 m/s north, a speed of 2.5 m/s. Turned right round at the same speed, −v is 3 m/s west and 4 m/s south, and its speed is still 5 m/s. The unit vector, v ÷ 5, is 0.6 east and 0.8 north: the heading with the speed taken out.

**Common mistakes**
- Treating a moved arrow as a new vector. If the moves match, it is the same vector.
- Writing BA = AB. They are the same size but point opposite ways, so BA = −AB.
- Forgetting that a minus number turns the arrow round. −2a points the other way from a.
- Giving a negative size. −2a has size 10, not −10.
- Making a unit vector by dividing by the moves added together. For 6 across and 8 up, dividing by 14 gives a size near 0.71, not 1. Divide by the size, 10.
- Calling a speed a velocity. 12 knots is a speed. 12 knots due east is a velocity.

sources.quote: A vector is a mathematical object that has both a magnitude (length) and a direction. Vectors can be used to represent physical quantities such as velocity, force, and acceleration.
